papers.title: Childhood and adolescent changes in sleep spindle trends across the night.
papers.abstract: Sleep spindle trends across sleep cycles provide clues to factors that influence these distinct EEG waveforms. We describe cycle trends in spindle density, frequency, amplitude, and duration, and we determine how these trends change across childhood and adolescence. Furthermore, we test how the trends in spindle density are related to trends in slow wave (delta) EEG incidence. A computer program detected and measured sleep spindles in central and frontal EEG from 1944 nights from our longitudinal dataset of semiannual recordings from 97 participants, ages 6-18 years. Spindle density and duration increased steeply between cycles 1 and 2 with smaller increases across subsequent cycles. The magnitude of these increases decreased with age. The spindle density cycle trend was strongly related to the delta cycle trend, but the age-related change in the density trend was not related to changes in delta. Spindle wave frequency shifted from an increase across cycles in children to a u-shaped trend in older adolescents, whereas central spindle amplitude shifted from a u-shaped trend to a linear increase. The trends in frontal and central spindles were, on the whole, similar with exceptions suggesting later maturation of frontal circuits. The age-related changes in sleep spindle measures across sleep cycles cannot be attributed solely to thalamocortical pruning but must also be affected by myelination and circuit reorganization. The age-related changes in cycle trends for spindle frequency indicate a shift from a strong homeostatic influence in children to greater circadian influence in late adolescence.

papers.title: Collapse of local circuit integrated information Φ during NREM sleep.
papers.abstract: Clarifying the mechanisms underlying the emergence of consciousness remains a fundamental challenge in modern neuroscience. Integrated Information Theory (IIT) provides a mathematical framework derived from the phenomenological properties of consciousness as its axioms. IIT proposes that consciousness is identical to a system's intrinsic cause-effect information structure, quantified by integrated information Φ. While IIT predicts that the Φ of a neuronal system should decrease during the loss of consciousness, this hypothesis has remained untested at the neural circuit level. The present study provides empirical support for this IIT prediction. It was found that Φ within local circuits decreases during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep compared to wakefulness (and REM sleep in the frontal cortex), regardless of cortical laminar structure. The reduction in Φ was particularly pronounced during OFF-periods, when neural activity is collectively suppressed. These results align with IIT's framework, suggesting that the loss of consciousness corresponds to a collapse of integrated information within local circuits. The findings provide empirical support for IIT as a mathematical theory aiming to explain conscious experiences.

Found that local-circuit Φ decreased during NREM compared to wakefulness (and frontal cortex REM), especially during OFF-periods, supporting the hypothesis that loss of consciousness corresponds to collapse of integrated information in local circuits.

papers.title: Hidden Drowsiness in Wakefulness: Differences in Resting-State EEG Profiles in Natural Short Sleepers Versus Recommended Length Sleepers.
papers.abstract: Chronic insufficient sleep affects cardiovascular, endocrine, immune and nervous systems and is linked to cognitive decline and increased mortality. Among habitual short sleepers, a subgroup known as natural short sleepers (NSS) report sleeping ≤ 6 h per night without experiencing subjective daytime dysfunction. However, discrepancies between subjective and objective markers of alertness raise questions about their true cognitive state. NSS have been described as high in behavioural activation, a phenotype overlapping with ADHD and mania in which dysregulation of resting-state brain arousal has been well documented. Despite these parallels, few studies have investigated the neurophysiological features of NSS. The current study examined resting-state EEG in NSS and recommended-length sleepers (RLS) during eyes-open conditions. Results showed that NSS exhibited significantly higher global alpha power and regionally steeper aperiodic exponents, particularly in occipital areas, both markers of increased drowsiness. Although global exponent values did not differ significantly, a significant Group × Region interaction was observed and NSS showed a trend toward increasing aperiodic exponents over time, suggesting less stable wakefulness under low-stimulation conditions. These findings point to subtle neurophysiological differences in NSS, raising the possibility that their perceived resilience to short sleep may mask underlying drowsiness.

papers.title: Episodic memory consolidation by reactivation of human concept neurons during sleep reflects contents, not sequence of events.
papers.abstract: How do our brains manage to store our everyday experiences into memory? Neurons in the human temporal lobe that respond to the concept of an individual person or object have been shown to provide the semantic building blocks for episodic memory. Recording from 1415 neurons in neurosurgical patients who learned a story involving specific concepts, we found reactivation of neurons representing these concepts during slow-wave sleep after learning. Concept neurons were conjointly reactivated, particularly during sharp-wave ripples, with time lags suitable for synaptic modification. However, the temporal sequence of reactivation did not reflect the sequence of concepts in the learned story. Unlike rodent place cells, which can acquire preferred firing locations during exploration of new environments according to their pre-existing preferred sequence of activation, human concept neurons are tuned to specific semantic contents before learning starts. Consequently, pre-existing firing sequences correlate with consecutive place fields in rodents, but not with sequences of events in human experience. Thus, in contrast to reactivation of rodent place cells, reactivation of human concept cells does not reflect sequences of events in human experience.

papers.title: Sleep changes what memories become: Post-learning sleep reduces forgetting following delayed reactivation.
papers.abstract: Sleep supports memory consolidation, yet most studies assess retention within hours or one day, leaving unclear whether an initial post-learning sleep episode continues to shape memory after several sleep-wake cycles. We examined whether these effects remain detectable one week later and whether they emerge following delayed memory reactivation. In Study 1, participants learned 30 sound-word associations and then completed a short nap, remained awake, or took a longer nap that included both non-rapid eye movement and rapid eye movement sleep. Memory was tested seven days later. All groups showed substantial forgetting, with no significant differences between groups. In Study 2, participants completed the same task followed by either a short nap or wakefulness. Six days later, the associations were reactivated using an incomplete reminder, and memory was tested the following day. Participants who had slept after learning showed less forgetting than those who had remained awake. Within the nap group, greater slow-wave sleep duration, stronger slow-oscillation activity, and a higher number of fast spindles were associated with better memory performance after reactivation. These findings suggest that post-learning sleep can influence the later expression of declarative memories even when no advantage is evident at delayed testing alone. An early sleep episode may therefore shape how a memory responds to subsequent reactivation, extending the influence of sleep-dependent consolidation beyond immediate retention.

papers.title: Periodic generalized nonepileptiform discharges (PGNDs) during NREM sleep before nocturnal seizures in temporal and extratemporal lobe epilepsy: An exploratory quantitative EEG study.
papers.abstract: To explore whether the spectral power of periodic generalized nonepileptiform discharges (PGNDs), a newly operationalized subset of CAP A-like NREM slow-wave events, differs between temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) and extratemporal lobe epilepsy (ETLE), and to identify demographic, clinical, and etiological factors associated with delta power. We retrospectively analyzed drug-resistant focal epilepsy patients undergoing long-term video-EEG monitoring (2018-2024) with at least two PGNDs in the preictal period of nocturnal seizures. PGNDs were visually scored and subtyped, and matched interictal NREM controls were selected. Absolute and relative (amplitude-normalized) spectral power was calculated for five frequency bands. Analyses were performed at the patient level, with false discovery rate (FDR) correction, cross-validated ROC analysis, confounder-adjusted models, and a mixed-effects model for determinants of delta power. Sixty-eight patients (35 TLE, 33 ETLE; 124 seizures, 711 PGNDs) met inclusion criteria. Delta (0.5-2.4 Hz) power of the PGND just before seizure onset (PGND1) was higher in ETLE than TLE, both in absolute terms (p = 0.016) and relative to total power (51.6% vs. 45.1%, p = 0.006, FDR q = 0.035), and the difference persisted after adjustment for carbamazepine use. Discrimination was modest (AUC=0.669; leave-one-out sensitivity 61%, specificity 74%). Absolute electrode-level differences did not survive FDR correction, whereas relative PGND1 delta power remained higher in ETLE at 16 of 20 electrodes after correction, indicating a widespread rather than regional difference. No within-patient preictal increase in PGND power was observed. Only febrile seizure history was independently associated with delta power. PGND delta power differs between ETLE and TLE independently of overall EEG amplitude, suggesting localization-related differences in NREM slow-wave events rather than a preictal biomarker. Given the modest discrimination and exploratory design, validation in independent cohorts is required before any clinical application.

papers.title: Protocol-aware dual-view single-channel EEG sleep staging with improved N1 discrimination on public sleep-EDF and SHHS benchmarks.
papers.abstract: To develop and evaluate DualViewSeqSleepNet, a protocol-aware single-channel EEG model for automatic sleep staging under reproducible public benchmark settings. The model integrates raw-waveform and spectral encoders, gated epoch-level fusion, lightweight bidirectional cross-epoch aggregation, and an auxiliary loss targeting Wake-N1 and N1-N2 transitions. Primary testing used the exact Sleep-EDF SC-subset protocol of SeriesSleepNet. Secondary no-retuning evaluation used SHHS-1 healthy C4-A1 data. On Sleep-EDF, DualViewSeqSleepNet achieved macro-F1 0.821, accuracy 0.869, and Cohen's kappa 0.808, exceeding the SeriesSleepNet anchor and improving N1 F1 from 0.506 to 0.535. On SHHS-1, it reached macro-F1 0.791 and accuracy 0.854 without architecture-family retuning. Ablation and robustness analyses supported the contributions of dual-view fusion, cross-epoch aggregation, and N1-aware supervision. DualViewSeqSleepNet provides a modest, protocol-aligned improvement for public single-channel sleep staging, especially near Wake-N1-N2 boundaries, but does not establish external clinical validation or autonomous deployment readiness.

papers.title: High-Density EEG Signatures of Cataplexy in Narcolepsy Type 1.
papers.abstract: Cataplexy, the pathognomonic symptom of narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), consists of sudden, emotion-triggered episodes of muscle atonia during wakefulness, with preserved consciousness. Although cataplexy shares features with REM sleep, its neurophysiological nature remains incompletely understood, particularly in humans. We investigated the electrophysiological signature of cataplexy using 128-channels EEG polysomnography in 10 drug-free NT1 adults. We analyzed 73 cataplexy epochs of ~30 seconds from 59 recorded episodes, compared with epochs of quiet wakefulness, N1 sleep, tonic and phasic REM, and direct-entry-REM-sleep. We compared hypnodensity profiles, computed with U-Sleep, of cataplexy and reference states. Regional and topographic spectral power across delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands, absolute and relative to total power, were compared across states. EEG fingerprint robustness was assessed via within- and between-participant correlation distances. Cataplexy exhibited a distinct EEG profile with intermediate sleep-wake spectral features. Relative power showed scalp-wide reduced beta and increased delta-theta versus wakefulness, alongside elevated posterior beta and scalp-wide reduced theta-delta versus sleep. Absolute power showed increased global field power across most bands, supporting REM-like activity superimposed onto wake desynchronization. Hypnodensity analysis revealed a mixed-state signature combining wake-, REM-, and N1-like probabilities, supporting a hybrid state. Cataplexy differed from direct-entry-REM-sleep, arguing against a simple wake-to-REM transition. Variability analyses indicated greater between-participants than within-participant differences, suggesting partially conserved but individually expressed EEG signatures. Our findings support that cataplexy is a dissociated hybrid brain state reflecting co-activation of REM-like and wake-like synchronizations, constituting a unique pathological state with intermediate electrophysiological features.

Signatures varied more between than within participants, supporting a dissociated hybrid brain state distinct from direct wake-to-REM transition.

papers.title: BDNF-mediated amelioration of sleep disruption-induced behavioral disorders by Ginkgo biloba.
papers.abstract: Sleep disruptions linked to adverse outcomes ranging from cognitive decline (e.g., in memory, learning, and sensory integration) to emotional dysregulation (e.g., stress and pathological anxiety). Although pre-sleep cognitive engagement may alleviate some of these effects, effective pharmacological interventions are needed. Ginkgo biloba, a dietary supplement, exerts broad pharmacological actions that support neural function. Here, we investigate hypothesis that Ginkgo biloba counteracts sleep deprivation's detrimental effects by promoting BDNF-dependent neuroplasticity, thereby restoring cognitive and emotional homeostasis. Twenty-eight male Wistar rats were randomly assigned to four groups: sleep disruption (SD) followed by Ginkgo biloba extract (250 mg/kg i.p.), sleep-disrupted group only, extract only, and control. The Ginkgo biloba collected from botanical garden of Tehran and the extract was prepared via percolation of plant material with ethanol, followed by evaporation and reconstitution. Animals were subjected to multiple-platform-induced sleep disruption (MPSD) for 2 h/day for 3 consecutive days. Behavioral assessments included the open-field test for stress/anxiety and the Barnes maze for spatial learning and memory over three days. Hippocampal BDNF levels were quantified using ELISA. Intraperitoneal Ginkgo biloba extract improved learning in sleep-disrupted rats, reducing probe-day latency from 71 ± 11 s (deprived) to 38 ± 8 s (p < 0.001); Ginkgo biloba alone yielded 15 ± 8 s. The open-field test revealed a significant increase in both locomotor speed and total distance traveled in the sleep-disrupted rats compared with the other experimental groups (P < 0.001). Sleep disruption reduced hippocampal BDNF from 544.55 ± 23-381.19 ± 17 pm/ml (p < 0.0001). Ginkgo biloba treatment significantly prevented this reduction (557 ± 27 pm/ml; p < 0.001) and, when administered alone, increased BDNF by 20% compared to controls (653 ± 25 pm/ml). Sleep disruption impaired memory and learning but did not significantly affect anxiety. Treatment with Ginkgo biloba extract (250 mg/kg) improved memory and reduced anxiety. Hippocampal BDNF changes suggest restorative effects may be mediated by increasing BDNF levels reduced by deprivation. As an Iranian Ginkgo biloba extract was used, further research is needed to identify optimal extraction methods and phytochemical compositions for enhancing BDNF levels, thereby optimizing therapeutic potential of Ginkgo biloba -derived compounds for sleep and cognitive applications.

Ginkgo biloba treatment also improved memory and reduced anxiety.

papers.title: Actimetry-Derived Sleep and Circadian Parameters in a Population-Based Sample from São Paulo: Findings from the EPISONO Cohort.
papers.abstract: To set benchmarks for sleep estimates and for parameters of rest-activity, light exposure, and skin temperature rhythms in a cohort from São Paulo. The present study used data from the 4th edition of the São Paulo Epidemiologic Sleep Study (Estudo Epidemiológico do Sono da cidade de São Paulo, EPISONO, in Portuguese), conducted between 2018 and 2019 ( N = 769). A subset of 404 participants (60% female; mean age: 49.42 ± 14.90 years) was selected based on standardized 7-day records (5 weekdays and 2 free days). Sleep estimates, cosine-based and nonparametric parameters, were extracted and added as dependent variables in generalized linear models to investigate the effects of age, sex, body mass index, socioeconomic status, season of data collection and daylight-saving time on it. Participants aged 40 years or older had earlier sleep, circadian and light exposure timing, and reduced activity levels and amplitude. Females slept longer than males and exhibited a more stable and less fragmented rest-activity rhythm but displayed impaired patterns of exposure to light. Lower socioeconomic status was associated with poorer sleep quality yet less disrupted rhythms. Obesity was correlated with greater instability in the rest-activity rhythm. Seasonal differences revealed that sleep was shorter and later in the spring compared with winter. Our results established reference values for actimetry parameters in the largest city in Latin America and can be applied to similar urban populations. They also highlight vulnerable subgroups with impaired sleep and circadian patterns in this understudied context. These findings can inform public health policies and guide the design of personalized interventions.

papers.title: Combination acetazolamide and supplemental oxygen markedly improves ventilatory control instability and OSA severity.
papers.abstract: Ventilatory control instability (elevated 'loop gain') is a key pathophysiological determinant of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), but available interventions have modest potency. Since acetazolamide (ACZ) and supplemental oxygen (O2) independently lower loop gain via different mechanisms, can combination ACZO2 strongly reduce loop gain and therefore OSA severity? In a randomized, single-blind, crossover trial, 22 participants with moderate-severe OSA (15 M, 7 F), received ACZ (500 mg daily) or placebo for 7 days. On the final nights of each period, participants underwent two nights of polysomnography with O2 (3 L/min) or sham. Loop gain (LG1) and flow-based apnea-hypopnea-index (fAHI, events scored without desaturation/arousal criteria) were assessed from polysomnography at each visit. Compared with placebo+sham both ACZ and O2 monotherapies produced significant reduction in both LG1 and AHI. Combination ACZO2 markedly reduced LG1 by -0.26 [CI95%: -0.32, -0.20], and further significantly reduced LG1 compared to both ACZ (-0.07 [-0.13, -0.01]) and O2 alone -0.08 [-0.14, -0.02]. ACZO2 strongly reduced fAHI by -23.3/hr [-26.6, -13.1] (-55.2% [-63.9, -44.4]), however was not superior to ACZ alone (-3.4/h [-8.5, 1.6], -14.6% [-31.1, 5.8]). In patients with OSA, combining acetazolamide and supplemental oxygen provides a potent reduction in loop gain and roughly halves the AHI. This combination intervention holds promise for individuals whose OSA is meaningfully driven by elevated ventilatory control. ACTRN12616001297415.

papers.title: Circadian Disruption and Chrono-rehabilitation After Spinal Cord Injury.
papers.abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) disrupts circadian biology through multiple mechanisms, including dysregulation of core clock genes, inversion of melatonin secretion rhythms, blunted thermoregulatory oscillations, and loss of autonomic pathways that relay timing signals from the suprachiasmatic nucleus to peripheral tissues. These disruptions affect the processes on which rehabilitation depends, that is, neuroplasticity, motor learning consolidation, inflammatory modulation, and tissue repair. Despite this, circadian assessment and intervention remain absent from standard SCI rehabilitation protocols. It can be argued that restoring temporal organization is not ancillary to SCI rehabilitation but is a prerequisite for optimizing functional recovery. However, the evidence underpinning many of the proposed interventions is largely derived from non-SCI populations or preclinical models, and direct clinical trial data in SCI rehabilitation remain limited. Herein, the authors propose a chronobiological framework for SCI rehabilitation that includes systematic sleep-wake assessment using actigraphy and validated questionnaires, timed bright light therapy, individually dosed melatonin supplementation, and scheduling of intensive therapy sessions during patients' peak neurocognitive and motor performance windows. The integration of circadian medicine into SCI rehabilitation requires a shift in perspective; patients are not temporally neutral and their recovery potential is modulated by circadian function.

papers.title: Impact of intermittent hypoxia on drug-metabolizing enzymes and transporters and drug pharmacokinetics: an underestimated concern in obstructive sleep apnea patients?
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSA) is a prevalent and life-threatening respiratory disease. Marked by intermittent hypoxia (IH) and chronic inflammation, OSA frequently co-occurs with comorbidities like hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia or depression, necessitating various medications. However, the response to some treatments is notably compromised in OSA patients, manifesting as reduced efficacy and/or increased incidence of adverse events. The mechanisms underlying this altered pharmacological response remain unelucidated. Although comorbidities may substantially contribute to these alterations, IH and inflammation, key features of OSA, are known to modify drug-metabolizing enzymes and transporters (DMETs). We therefore hypothesized that OSA/IH may affect DMETs, thereby altering drug pharmacokinetics and drug response. This narrative review synthesizes existing literature regarding the impact of OSA/IH on DMETs and pharmacokinetics both in experimental models and human, along with the underlying mechanisms exploring the roles of pro-inflammatory cytokines, transcription factors and epigenetics. Subsequently, we discuss the potential consequences of these IH-induced DMETs alterations on drug response in OSA patient population. In this purpose, we examine the hypothesis of pharmacokinetic modifications for each drug (or pharmacotherapeutic class) whose response appears altered in OSA patients. Additionally, we analyze the pharmacokinetic profile of the most commonly dispensed medications in OSA patients in order to identify additional drugs whose efficacy or safety might be compromised by IH-induced DMETs alterations. Finally, in the absence of conclusive clinical evidence, we propose priority research areas to better characterize the impact of OSA/IH on DMETs, pharmacokinetics, and drug response, and the underlying mechanisms.

papers.title: Effects of Circadian Disruption and Chronotype on Postural Stability During Quiet Stance.
papers.abstract: Postural control is fundamental for daily activities and is known to be sensitive to disruptions of the circadian system. The present study investigated how individual circadian alignment influences postural stability in healthy adults. In total, 39 participants wore actigraphs for 2 weeks to obtain circadian regularity and misalignment parameters: composite phase deviation (CPD), interdaily stability (IS), and intradaily variability (IV). Chronotype was assessed from corrected midsleep time on free days. Postural stability was evaluated through center of pressure (COP) trajectories recorded while the participant stood on a force platform under different sensory conditions. Postural dynamics were analyzed using both linear sway measures and recurrence quantification analysis, with particular focus on laminarity (LAM) and trapping time (TT) as indicators of postural control stability and adaptability. Higher circadian disruption, reflected by increased CPD and reduced IS, was associated with greater postural instability, characterized by increased sway magnitude and higher values of LAM and TT, suggesting more intermittent and less adaptive postural control strategies. Additionally, individuals with later chronotypes exhibited poorer postural stability compared with those with earlier chronotypes. Therefore, these findings indicate that circadian disruption is associated with alterations in postural control dynamics, potentially reducing the adaptability of the postural system. Even in healthy adults, irregular sleep-wake patterns may place the sensorimotor system in a suboptimal state, increasing vulnerability to balance impairments.

papers.title: Pharmacological and non-pharmacological management of sleep disturbances in Alzheimer's disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: BackgroundSleep disturbances affect half of Alzheimer's disease patients, accelerating cognitive decline and increasing caregiver burden. The comparative effectiveness of available interventions remains unclear.ObjectiveTo compare pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions on sleep outcomes in Alzheimer's disease using network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs).MethodsFollowing PRISMA and a registered PROSPERO protocol (CRD420250653178), four databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, Web of Science) were searched through July 2026 for RCTs. Pairwise and frequentist random-effects network meta-analyses using Hedges' g were performed for six sleep outcomes: total sleep time (TST), wake after sleep onset (WASO), nocturnal awakenings (NoA), sleep efficiency, daytime sleep, and daytime naps. A Bayesian network meta-analysis served as a sensitivity analysis.ResultsTwelve RCTs (N = 936, 32 study arms) were included. Zolpidem and zopiclone reduced sleep fragmentation, with improvements in NoA (SMD -1.09) and WASO (SMD -0.86), although these findings were based on a single short-term trial. Suvorexant increased TST (SMD 0.376) and increased TST (SMD 0.376), while lemborexant 2.5 mg reduced NoA (SMD -0.98), with favorable short-term tolerability. Walking (SMD -0.48), bright light therapy (SMD -0.37), and NITE-AD (SMD -0.52) reduced NoA, while combined light therapy and melatonin reduced daytime sleep (SMD -0.858). Melatonin monotherapy, trazodone, and mirtazapine showed limited or inconsistent effects.ConclusionsNon-pharmacological interventions may be considered before pharmacological treatment. When pharmacotherapy is required, dual orexin receptor antagonists may be useful for selected sleep outcomes, whereas Z-drugs should be used cautiously given their established safety concerns. Larger, longer-duration head-to-head trials using standardized sleep outcomes are needed.

Non-pharmacological approaches (walking, bright light therapy, NITE-AD) reduced nocturnal awakenings, while dual orexin receptor antagonists improved total sleep time and Z-drugs reduced sleep fragmentation but with safety concerns, supporting non-pharmacological treatment first.

papers.title: Preserved social development but impaired executive function in a Shank3 -deficient rat model of Phelan-McDermid syndrome.
papers.abstract: Phelan-McDermid syndrome (PMS) is a genetic neurodevelopmental disorder caused by a microdeletion within chromosome 22q13.3 1-6 , and accounts for ∼1-3% of cases of autism spectrum disorders (ASD). Individuals with PMS typically present with neonatal hypotonia, severe speech delay, intellectual disability, motor impairments, and autism-related features, although additional manifestations such as epilepsy, sleep disturbances, and developmental regression are common. As in ASD, there is considerable heterogeneity in cognitive and behavioral impairments in PMS, making it difficult to determine which features arise directly from SHANK3/Shank3 deficiency and how deficits manifest across development. In the present study, we transferred the targeted Shank3 mutation, previously characterized on the Sprague Dawley background, onto the Long-Evans strain and performed a longitudinal behavioral assessment of Shank3 -deficient rats from infancy to adulthood. The rats were evaluated for delays in early sensory and motor development, and ultrasonic vocalizations as neonates, social behavior, short term memory and gait as juveniles, and cognitive-executive dysfunction using a touchscreen-based visual discrimination and reversal learning task as adults. Despite profound reductions and/or complete loss of Shank3 protein expression, heterozygous and homozygous male and female rats showed normal physical and neurological reflexes across development, yet female Shank3 knockout pups showed a selective reduction in distress-associated ultrasonic vocalizations. As juveniles, subtle abnormalities emerged in short-term memory and limb coordination, while social preference for novelty and recognition was normal. Prominent behavioral abnormalities were observed in adults characterized by rapid and error-prone responding to visual stimuli during discrimination learning and reversal. papers.title: EEG biomarkers for neurodegenerative diseases: Machine learning applications and clinical trial insights.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) are diverse conditions characterised by selective dysfunction and progressive loss of neurons, glial cells, and neural networks in the brain and spinal cord. NDs pose a major global health challenge due to ageing populations and lack of cure, prompting interest in developing algorithms for early detection and biomarkers. Electroencephalography (EEG), a non-invasive and cost-effective tool, has emerged as a promising method for identifying neural signatures of NDs. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) have further enabled automated diagnosis, disease monitoring, and prognostic modelling using EEG data. This review synthesises evidence from 226 studies, mapping the current landscape of EEG-based diagnosis, prognosis, and patient stratification across various NDs. Unlike prior reviews, it provides a comprehensive overview across multiple disorders, including rare ones, and evaluates the role of ML and AI in clinical translation. We analyse research trends, EEG acquisition and preprocessing, and the development of biomarkers for disease diagnosis, prognosis, treatment monitoring, and patient stratification. Spectral power, event-related potentials, and connectivity are the main features, with support vector machines and neural networks as the primary classifiers. We review clinical trials involving EEG in NDs and highlight open-source EEG repositories to support reproducibility and data sharing. Despite promising results, challenges such as small sample sizes, methodological differences, limited model interpretability, and gaps in clinical validation remain. The review highlights the potential of EEG combined with ML/AI for early diagnosis and therapy, while outlining future directions through standardised pipelines, explainable models, and collaborative open data initiatives.

papers.title: Transformer-based EEG source imaging localizes pathological high-frequency oscillations in focal epilepsy.
papers.abstract: High-frequency oscillations are specific biomarkers of the epileptogenic zone, yet their non-invasive localization from scalp EEG remains challenging due to their brief duration, low amplitude and poor signal-to-noise ratio. Here, we introduce a transformer-based high-frequency oscillation deep source-imaging framework (TH-DeepSIF) trained on biologically realistic neural mass model simulations for non-invasive high-frequency oscillation source imaging. The model was evaluated in simulated single- and dual-source scenarios, where it recovered both the spatial location and temporal dynamics of high-frequency oscillation generators under increasing spatiotemporal complexity. We further validated TH-DeepSIF in 20 patients with drug-resistant epilepsy by comparing reconstructed high-frequency oscillation sources with surgical resection regions. TH-DeepSIF achieved accurate localization and waveform reconstruction in simulations, demonstrating low localization error and strong temporal correspondence with ground truth. In clinical data, pathological high-frequency oscillations (spike ripples) showed strong agreement with resection regions, with a median localization error of 10.9 mm and specificity of 0.883. In a subset of six patients with intracranial EEG, pathological high-frequency oscillation source estimates were spatially close to the seizure onset zone (median localization error: 2.41 mm). Compared with all detected high-frequency oscillations, imaging based on pathological high-frequency oscillations yielded significantly improved spatial correspondence and performance across multiple metrics. Reconstructed source activity was also temporally aligned with both scalp high-frequency oscillation bursts and associated spike deflections. These results demonstrate that TH-DeepSIF provides a data-driven framework for non-invasive high-frequency oscillation source imaging with improved anatomical specificity and support the use of pathological high-frequency oscillations as informative biomarkers for epileptogenic zone localization.

papers.title: Environmental noise and cardiometabolic health: a transatlantic perspective.
papers.abstract: Environmental noise is a pervasive but under-recognized cardiovascular and metabolic risk factor. Drawing on prior expert reviews and large-scale epidemiologic and mechanistic studies, this review synthesizes evidence on the burden, major clinical associations, biological pathways, vulnerable populations, and mitigation strategies relevant to cardiovascular health. Road traffic noise is consistently and dose-dependently associated with higher risks of ischaemic heart disease, stroke, heart failure, diabetes, sleep disturbance, and adverse mental health outcomes, whereas for railway and aircraft noise, the evidence base is less consistent, although important associations are increasingly reported. Translational human imaging studies, controlled exposure experiments, and animal models converge on a common pathway in which chronic and intermittent noise exposure activates stress-responsive neural circuits, increases sympathetic and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activity, promotes oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and vascular inflammation, and may thereby accelerate cardiometabolic disease. Noise frequently co-occurs with air pollution, heat, and adverse social and built environments, particularly in socioeconomically disadvantaged communities, and these combined exposures may contribute additively to cardiovascular risk. These effects are especially relevant in urban populations with nighttime exposure and multiple co-exposures. Despite this growing evidence base, environmental noise remains largely absent from contemporary cardiovascular risk assessment tools, prevention guidelines, and routine patient counselling, representing a missed opportunity for risk reduction. Effective mitigation will require a hierarchical strategy combining source reduction, health-informed urban and transport planning, and targeted individual protection. Reducing environmental noise exposure should be recognized as an important opportunity to protect and advance cardiovascular and metabolic health in the 21st century.

papers.title: Seizure-like behaviors in a mutant mouse with increased calpain-dependent cleavage of αII-spectrin.
papers.abstract: Mutations inSPTAN1, the gene encoding the neuronal cytoskeletal protein αII-spectrin, are associated with epilepsy and movement disorders, complicating the clinical interpretation of seizure-like behaviors. Stress-induced paroxysmal motor events can mimic behaviors typically observed in epileptic seizures, yet they do not exhibit definitive electrophysiological correlates. Mutant and wild-type (WT) mice were subject to automated gait analysis, long-term video-EEG monitoring, and a handling-induced seizure susceptibility (HISS) paradigm at various ages. R1098Q mice demonstrated pronounced gait abnormalities characteristic of ataxia as well as age-related increases in delta and theta power, and spike-wave discharges (SWD), suggesting elevated network excitability. During the HISS test, nearly all mutant mice exhibited significant seizure-like motor responses, such as forelimb clonus, impaired balance, and falls, whereas WT mice displayed no abnormal reactions. Notably, these motor behaviors did not coincide with cortical ictal EEG activity. Rather, stress induced a transient suppression of cortical EEG spiking, followed by the return of interictal spiking and SWDs. The present findings demonstrate a dissociation between seizure-like behaviors and cortical ictal EEG activity inSptan1R1098Q mice. These findings emphasize the limitations inherent to classifying seizures based solely on behavioral observations and underscore the necessity of incorporating electrophysiological data when evaluating seizure-like manifestations in genetic epilepsy models characterized by significant motor dysfunction. Such differentiation holds substantial relevance for preclinical epilepsy research and informs the interpretation of seizure-like events within neurogenetic disorders.

papers.title: Comparative outcomes following virtual reality-assisted and traditional supplementary exercise programs and usual training on balance, sprint performance, and resting-state EEG in youth academy football players.
papers.abstract: This study compared outcomes associated with an eight-week virtual reality-assisted supplementary exercise program, a traditional supplementary exercise program, and usual training in youth-academy football players. Because the two active programs were not empirically matched for exercise content or exposure dose, the study was not designed to isolate a virtual-reality-specific effect. Thirty-nine male youth-academy football players (18.38 ± 0.49 years; n = 13/group) were randomly allocated to a virtual reality-assisted exercise group, a traditional exercise group, or a usual-training control group using manual block randomization performed by an independent researcher. Balance, 30-m sprint, resting-state spectral power, and anterior-central synchronization were assessed before and after the intervention. Baseline-adjusted ANCOVA was used to estimate post-intervention between-group differences because baseline imbalances were present. Mixed-design ANOVA time × group interactions were retained as complementary sensitivity analyses and corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure across nine retained interaction tests. Baseline-adjusted ANCOVA showed between-group differences in two-leg, dominant-leg, and non-dominant-leg balance. For two-leg balance, all three pairwise comparisons were statistically detectable. For dominant-leg and non-dominant-leg balance, adjusted post-test stability-index values were lower in the virtual reality-assisted group than in both the traditional and control groups; no statistically detectable difference was found between the traditional and control groups. The 30-m sprint showed an adjusted post-test difference between the virtual reality-assisted and control groups, but no differential pre-post trajectory was detected. An eight-week virtual reality-assisted supplementary exercise program was associated with greater improvements in two-leg, dominant-leg, and non-dominant-leg balance compared with traditional supplementary exercise and usual training in youth football players. Although a difference in 30-m sprint performance was observed between the virtual reality and control groups, no differential pre-post trajectory was detected. papers.title: Comparative efficacy of different digital technologies in adults with insomnia: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

Eligible studies enrolled adult participants with insomnia, with primary outcomes including the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Sleep Onset Latency (SOL), and Wake After Sleep Onset (WASO). Risk of bias was assessed using the RoB 2.0 tool. Intervention hierarchies were obtained using the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA). The GRADE framework for network meta-analysis was applied to rate evidence certainty. Twenty-six RCTs involving 6 353 participants covering eight digital interventions were included. Conventional meta-analysis showed that digital interventions significantly reduced ISI (MD = 3.31, 95%CI 2.48-4.15, P< 0.001, I²= 67%), improved PSQI (MD = 1.52, 95%CI 1.07-1.97, P < 0.001, I² = 0%), and shortened SOL (MD = 12.60, 95%CI 7.66-17.55, P < 0.001, I² = 0%) and WASO (MD = 16.93, 95%CI 8.90-24.96, P < 0.001, I² = 0%). Different digital technologies can significantly improve various sleep outcomes among adults with insomnia. DCBT-I showed favourable effect estimates. papers.title: Temporal dissociation across the eye-brain-muscle cascade delineates a preparation window before muscle activation in subacute stroke.
papers.abstract: Upper-limb motor impairment after stroke is compounded by a disrupted sensorimotor cascade linking visual attention, cortical motor preparation, and peripheral muscle activation. Whether these stages are temporally dissociated in subacute stroke, and whether their timing carries information about the preparation and execution of a reaching action, remains unclear. Thirty subacute stroke survivors and 30 healthy controls performed a full-plane nine-grid reaching task while eye-tracking, electroencephalography (EEG), and surface electromyography (EMG) were recorded synchronously. Three neurophysiological latencies were extracted: first fixation on the target, stimulus-locked lateralized readiness potential (s-LRP) onset, and peripheral muscle activation onset. Compared with controls, patients showed a stepwise delay across the cascade, with delayed visual engagement (616.73 ms vs. 367.86 ms) and delayed peripheral muscle activation (1,080 ms vs. 605 ms) bracketing a cortical preparation window. A random-forest classifier was trained on window-level gaze-timing features, computed separately for each target-presentation and inter-target interval of the task. Under participant-level leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, it achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.973 (95% CI 0.958-0.984) and an accuracy of 0.918, numerically the highest among the five classifiers compared. These findings describe a quantifiable temporal organization of the sensorimotor cascade in the subacute stage of stroke and indicate that gaze timing carries discriminative information about the occurrence of an instructed reaching action. They establish a descriptive, testable framework rather than a demonstrated clinical benefit. Validation in chronic stroke and across independent samples is further required.

This dataset was created to collect EEG signals from participants in three categories: (i) AD, (ii) FTD, and (iii) healthy control (HC). To automatically detect these groups, we proposed a new SOXFE model. This model includes a novel feature extraction function inspired by Tesla's 369 vortex and the Tree of Thought (ToT), termed the Tesla Tree of Thought Pattern (TToTP). In the feature selection phase, we applied cumulative weighted iterative neighborhood component analysis (CWINCA), to select the most informative features. In the classification phase, we employed the t algorithm-based k-nearest neighbors (tkNN). The fourth phase involves information fusion, where the results from each channel are voted on using iterative majority voting (IMV), and the best outcome is selected. The final phase is explainable results generation, in which a cortical channel map (CCMap) is created based on the findings from the information fusion phase.ResultsWe applied the TToTP-based SOXFE model to the EEG dementia dataset, achieving over 99% classification accuracy. Additionally, a cortical channel map was generated using the classification results.ConclusionsThe proposed TToTP-based SOXFE model achieved high classification performance and successfully generated a cortical channel map. The model contributes to both feature engineering and neuroscience.

All patients were randomly divided into two groups: one for model development (n = 209) and the other for internal validation (n = 89). Candidate variables were selected using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. Independent predictors were identified through multivariable logistic regression, and a predictive nomogram was constructed. The model's discriminatory ability, calibration performance, and clinical utility were evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, calibration plots, and decision curve analysis (DCA). papers.title: Nocturnal Sweating in Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Systematic Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is commonly associated with symptoms such as snoring and daytime sleepiness, while atypical manifestations including nocturnal sweating remain less clearly understood. However, more recent studies have suggested that nocturnal sweating may be associated with hypoxemic burden, rapid eye movement (REM)-related respiratory worsening, sleep fragmentation, and sympathetic nervous system activation rather than respiratory event frequency alone. Physiological studies have demonstrated improvement in sweating after continuous or automatic positive airway pressure therapy, supporting a reversible autonomic mechanism. An exploratory meta-analysis of three comparative studies showed a non-significant increase in nocturnal sweating among OSA patients (odds ratio [OR] = 1.85; 95%CI: 0.87-3.92; I 2 = 91.7%). papers.title: Perioperative esketamine is associated with attenuated sleep deprivation-related cognitive dysfunction: a retrospective biomarker cohort study of the ferroptosis-neuroinflammation axis.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation is common in older surgical patients and may increase vulnerability to postoperative neurocognitive dysfunction through oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and regulated cell-death pathways. Experimental studies increasingly implicate hippocampal ferroptosis, particularly disruption of the SLC7A11-GSH-GPX4 defense axis, in sleep-deprivation-related cognitive injury. Esketamine has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, but whether its perioperative neurocognitive benefit is associated with a ferroptosis-related molecular phenotype in clinical patients remains uncertain. We conducted a retrospective biomarker cohort study of 398 adults aged 60-80 years who underwent elective major non-cardiac surgery between January 2022 and December 2025. Patients were classified according to preoperative sleep deprivation (total sleep time <4 h and sleep efficiency <70% during the night before surgery) and perioperative esketamine exposure, generating four groups: NSD-C, NSD-E, SD-C, and SD-E. The primary outcome was early postoperative cognitive decline on postoperative day (POD) 7, defined by a ≥1-SD deterioration in a composite neuropsychological Z score. In a biomarker subcohort, plasma 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE), malondialdehyde (MDA), glutathione (GSH), glutathione peroxidase activity, inflammatory cytokines, neuronal injury markers, and PBMC expression of GPX4, SLC7A11, and ACSL4 were analyzed. Confounding was addressed using multivariable models and inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting. Bootstrap mediation models examined a ferroptosis-related redox score and IL-6 as candidate mediators. In the cohort, cognitive decline occurred in 32.5% of sleep-deprived patients without esketamine and 17.7% of sleep-deprived patients exposed to esketamine. After adjustment, esketamine exposure in the sleep-deprivation subgroup was associated with lower odds of cognitive decline (adjusted OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.26-0.92). Sleep deprivation was associated with higher 4-HNE, MDA, ACSL4, IL-6, TNF-α, and NSE and lower GSH, GPX activity, GPX4, and SLC7A11; these abnormalities were attenuated in the esketamine-exposed group. The exploratory ferroptosis-related redox score was independently associated with cognitive decline. Under the specified exploratory mediation model, the estimated total mediated proportion was 54%; this model-based decomposition does not establish causal biological mediation. Perioperative esketamine was associated with less pronounced early postoperative cognitive decline in sleep-deprived patients and a less pronounced peripheral ferroptosis-related/inflammatory phenotype.

papers.title: Metrics Reflecting Cumulative Exposure to Nocturnal Hypoxia Demonstrate Promising Performance in Distinguishing between Moderate and Severe Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
papers.abstract: The apnea-hypopnea index is traditionally used to classify the severity of obstructive sleep apnea; however, it does not fully capture the cumulative physiological impact of nocturnal hypoxia. Metrics that quantify integrated hypoxic exposure may provide a more accurate characterization of disease severity. The current study compared the independent association and discriminative performance of hypoxic burden, cumulative time with peripheral oxygen saturation below 90%, and oxygen desaturation frequency in distinguishing between moderate and severe obstructive sleep apnea. In total, 30 patients with moderate or severe disease were evaluated using actigraphy combined with continuous nocturnal oximetry. Separate logistic regression models adjusted for body mass index were developed. Hypoxic burden and cumulative time with peripheral oxygen saturation below 90% remained independently associated with severe disease, with odds ratios of 1.35 (95%CI: 1.05-1.75; p = 0.021) and 2.46 (95%CI: 1.03-5.90; p = 0.043) respectively, whereas desaturation frequency was not significant after adjustment (odds ratio: 1.90; 95%CI: 0.97-3.73; p = 0.061). The model including cumulative time with peripheral oxygen saturation below 90% yielded an area under the curve of 0.86 (95%CI: 0.728-0.996), while the models including hypoxic burden and desaturation frequency yielded values regarding the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of 0.84 (95%CI: 0.698-0.989) and 0.78 (95%CI: 0.618-0.954) respectively. These findings suggest good discriminative performance of metrics reflecting cumulative nocturnal hypoxic exposure; however, formal comparisons between the ROC curves were not performed. Metrics reflecting cumulative exposure to nocturnal hypoxia demonstrated promising performance in distinguishing between moderate and severe disease, and they may contribute to risk stratification in obstructive sleep apnea.

papers.title: Culturally Adapting a Behavioral Sleep Intervention for Older Korean Immigrants: A Community-Engaged Refinement Study.
papers.abstract: Older Korean immigrants experience high rates of chronic sleep difficulties, yet culturally tailored behavioral interventions are limited. This study aimed to refine a cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I)-based program for cultural relevance, acceptability, and usability. Five older Korean immigrants completed five in-person sessions of the SLEEP-OK program. Iterative refinements were informed by participant and stakeholder feedback, sleep educator field notes, and sleep diaries. Surface-structure adaptations addressed language, examples, and metaphors; deep-structure adaptations incorporated values, beliefs, and routines affecting sleep. All participants completed the program, reporting high acceptability and engagement. Modifications improved clarity, reduced burden, and integrated culturally relevant metaphors (e.g. "cooking kimchi stew," "untangling a knot"). Sleep educators found the sessions easy to deliver after adaptation. Culturally refining a behavioral sleep intervention for older Korean immigrants is feasible and acceptable, offering a model for adapting evidence-based sleep programs for linguistically and culturally diverse populations.

papers.title: Dupilumab for Moderate-to-Severe Chronic Prurigo Nodularis: A Retrospective Real-World Study of Effectiveness, Safety, and Prolonged Dosing Intervals.
papers.abstract: Chronic prurigo nodularis (CPN) is a multidimensional neuro-immunocutaneous disease characterized by severe, persistent pruritus, and the development of nodular lesions caused by repeated scratching, often associated with sleep disruption, psychological distress, and impaired quality of life. Dupilumab has demonstrated efficacy and safety in clinical trials, but evidence regarding the use of prolonged dosing intervals, and potential modifiers of response in real-world settings remains limited. We conducted a single-center, retrospective, observational study of adults with moderate-to-severe CPN treated with dupilumab in routine clinical practice. The primary endpoint was clinically meaningful pruritus improvement at week 24, defined as a ≥ 4-point reduction in Worst Itch-Numeric Rating Scale (WI-NRS). Secondary outcomes included achievement of Investigator's Global Assessment for Prurigo Nodularis-Stage (IGA PN-S) 0/1 and longitudinal changes in pruritus, nodular lesion burden, sleep disturbance, and quality of life. Adverse events, treatment discontinuation, exploratory baseline predictors of response, and patterns of dosing-interval extension and return to the standard every-2-week regimen were also recorded. In total, 26 patients were included. Median age at dupilumab initiation was 45.5 years (interquartile range [IQR] 33-53 years), and median follow-up was 50 weeks (IQR 32-62 years). Baseline disease burden was substantial, with severe itch, marked quality-of-life impairment, sleep disturbance, elevated impulsivity scores, and psychiatric comorbidity in 19 patients (73%). At week 24, 59% of patients achieved a ≥ 4-point WI-NRS reduction, while 45% achieved IGA PN-S 0/1 and combined WI-NRS-IGA PN-S response. A sustained improvement in itch, clinical severity, and quality of life was observed among evaluable patients through later follow-up. Prolongation of the dupilumab dosing interval was attempted in nine controlled responders and maintained without return to the standard regimen in five patients. Psychiatric comorbidity was associated with lower odds of WI-NRS response at week 24. Adverse events occurred in two patients (7.7%) and led to treatment withdrawal in one owing to gastrointestinal disorder. Dupilumab showed real-world effectiveness and a favorable safety profile in moderate-to-severe CPN. These findings support individualized, multidisciplinary management and further prospective investigation of response predictors and dosing-interval prolongation strategies. Scratching can keep the disease going, and many people also have sleep problems, emotional distress, and a major effect on daily life. Dupilumab is an injectable treatment that blocks two immune signals involved in inflammation and itch. Clinical trials have shown that dupilumab can help people with this disease, but less is known about how patients treated in everyday clinical practice will respond. In this study, we reviewed the medical records of 26 adults with moderate-to-severe CPN treated with dupilumab. After 24 weeks, 59% of patients who could be assessed had a meaningful reduction in worst itch, and in 45% the skin disease was clear or almost clear according to the doctor's assessment. Improvements in itch, skin signs, and quality of life generally continued during later follow-up. Overall, nine patients with good disease control were able to receive dupilumab less often; however, four needed to return to the standard every-2-week schedule. Side effects were uncommon and led to stopping treatment in one patient. Patients with mental health conditions seemed less likely to have a strong itch response, but this finding needs confirmation. These results support care that is tailored to each person, including mental health support when needed.

papers.title: Associations Between Marital Status and 24-Hr Movement Behaviors Among Older Adults: A Compositional Data Analysis With Gender-Stratified Findings.
papers.abstract: Marital status is a key social determinant of health and may influence older adults' movement behavior. Few studies have examined these associations using a compositional data framework or considered gender differences. We conducted a cross-sectional secondary analysis of accelerometer data from 814 older adults (mean age 68.9 ± 8.9 years; 59% women) in Wave 8 of the Survey of Health, Aging and Retirement in Europe. Twenty-four-hour movement behaviors, sedentary behavior (SB), light physical activity, moderate to vigorous physical activity (MVPA), and sleep were derived from Axivity AX3 accelerometers. Marital status was self-reported as "partnered" or "not partnered." Associations with 24-hr movement composition were examined using compositional multivariate linear regression based on isometric log-ratio coordinates, adjusting for age, sex, country, education, and body mass index. Sex-stratified models were also conducted. Partnered participants engaged in more MVPA and less SB than those not partnered. Not being partnered was associated with lower MVPA (β = -0.17; p = .031) and higher SB (β = 0.09; p = .030), with no differences in light physical activity or sleep. Sex-stratified analyses showed that not partnered men had higher light physical activity (β = 0.17; p = .020) and a trend toward lower MVPA. Among women, effects were smaller, though not among partnered women, who accumulated more SB (β = 0.12; p = .040). Marital status is linked to 24-hr movement in older adults, with not partnered individuals, particularly men, showing lower MVPA and higher SB. Significance/Implications: These results underline the need to support physical activity among single older adults and inform strategies for healthy aging.

papers.title: Mandibular advancement device vs continuous positive airway pressure in obstructive sleep apnea: An updated systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common sleep-related breathing disorder that increases the risk of cardiovascular diseases. While continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) remains the first-line therapy for OSA, adherence continues to be a major challenge. Recently, mandibular advancement devices (MADs) have emerged as a safe and effective alternative. This systematic review and meta-analysis aim to compare MAD and CPAP across several health outcomes. Following PRISMA guidelines, six databases were searched, and the protocol was preregistered on PROSPERO (CRD420251081182). Primary outcomes included apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), minimum peripheral capillary oxygen saturation (SpO2), oxygen desaturation index (ODI), and several blood pressure (BP) parameters. Secondary outcomes included adherence, BMI, among others. A meta-analysis was performed using R version 4.6.0 and heterogeneity was assessed using I2 statistics. A total of 18 studies were included with 1244 participants. The CPAP group showed improvement in SpO2 (MD = -4.54, 95% CI: -5.50 to -3.59; p < 0.01; I2 = 50.2%), ODI (MD = 6.54, 95% CI: 3.70 to 9.38; p < 0.01; I2 = 85.4%), and arousal index (MD = 4.40, 95% CI: 1.22 to 7.58; p = <0.01; I2 = 77.5%). The MAD group showed significantly greater adherence (MD = 1.43, 95% CI: 1.10 to 1.77; p < 0.01; I2 = 55.6%) and modest significant reduction in several BP parameters. Meta-regression identified baseline AHI as a significant moderator of treatment effect (β = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.30 to 1.35; p < 0.01). This review suggests that treatment selection between CPAP and MAD may be informed by OSA severity and expected adherence. CPAP remains superior in improving polysomnographic parameters. Further long-term trials incorporating objectively monitored adherence and hard cardiovascular outcomes are needed to guide individualized treatment selection in OSA.

papers.title: Short-term multidimensional effects of continuous positive airway pressure in patients with obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome: a single-center retrospective study.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the short-term effects of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) combined with conventional lifestyle intervention on sleep parameters, inflammatory status, hemorheology, vascular endothelial function, upper airway dimensions, and quality of life in patients with obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS). Medical records of 89 patients with obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS) treated between July 2023 and September 2025 were retrospectively reviewed. According to management methods, patients were divided into a control group (n=47; receiving lifestyle intervention alone) or a study group (n=42; receiving CPAP plus lifestyle intervention). After 12-week intervention, overall clinical response rates, apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), lowest oxygen saturation (LSaO2), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), upper airway cross-sectional areas, hemorheological parameters, inflammatory cytokines, endothelial function markers, and World Health Organization Quality of Life-BREF questionnaire (WHOQOL-BREF) scores were compared between groups. The overall response rate was higher in the study group than in the control group (92.86% vs. 42.55%, P < 0.001). After treatment, both groups showed improvements in AHI, LSaO2, PSQI, hemorheological parameters, inflammatory cytokines, endothelial function, and quality-of-life scores, with generally greater improvements in the study group (all P < 0.05). Upper airway cross-sectional areas increased in both groups, but between-group differences were not significant. CPAP combined with lifestyle intervention was associated with greater short-term improvements in sleep-related parameters, inflammation, hemorheology, endothelial function, and quality of life in patients with OSAHS. Larger prospective multicenter studies are needed to confirm these findings.

papers.title: Acupuncture and related needling in sports-related knee rehabilitation: a narrative review of neurophysiological mechanisms and assessment methods.
papers.abstract: Sports-related knee injuries, including anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture, patellofemoral pain (PFP), meniscal injury, and post-traumatic knee osteoarthritis (KOA), are not only problems of local tissue damage. They can alter joint afferent input, quadriceps activation, cortical control, confidence during return-to-sport, and long-term function. For this reason, knee rehabilitation in athletes need to consider both tissue healing and neurophysiological recovery. Manual acupuncture, electroacupuncture (EA), and trigger point dry needling (DN) have been investigated as adjunctive therapies for knee pain and rehabilitation. Manual acupuncture and EA are needle-based interventions derived from traditional Chinese medicine. DN is included here because of its relevance to musculoskeletal rehabilitation, rather than as a traditional Chinese medicine intervention. Clinical studies suggest possible improvements in pain, swelling, range of motion, self-reported function, and neuromuscular performance. Mechanistic studies also suggest effects on cortical hemodynamics, sensorimotor oscillations, descending pain modulation, spinal excitability, muscle activity, and arthrogenic muscle inhibition (AMI). However, direct evidence specifically in sports-related knee injury populations remains limited. This review discusses evidence from functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), electroencephalography (EEG), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), electromyography (EMG), clinical acupuncture research, and sports rehabilitation. We group the possible mechanisms into cortical intended, corticospinal or spinal-reflexive, and peripheral muscular levels. This framework is intended to guide future research rather than to imply established causality. Given the limited direct evidence currently available in sports-related knee populations, this review is intentionally hypothesis-generating in nature. Its primary value lies in synthesizing indirect evidence from related fields, constructing a testable mechanistic framework, and proposing concrete experimental designs to inform future research.

papers.title: A dynamic network analysis of anxiety-related distress within a quality-of-life framework among adults undergoing chemotherapy.
papers.abstract: To understand anxiety-related distress within the quality-of-life context, this study examined how anxiety-related distress is positioned in the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire (EORTC QLQ) framework, and assessed its strongest associations with other quality-of-life factors over time. This secondary analysis of randomized controlled trial data included 390 adults aged ≥ 50 years (63.1% female) who were assessed across six time points: before chemotherapy (baseline, T1) and during chemotherapy (T2-T6). Longitudinal network analysis was used to evaluate the position and associations of anxiety-related distress, represented by worry and tension, within the EORTC-QLQ framework. A baseline network using all 30 EORTC-QLQ items first identified the position of anxiety-related distress. A reduced longitudinal network using key nodes was then estimated to examine contemporaneous, between-person, and temporal associations over time. The baseline network revealed that worry played a central bridging role within the quality-of-life framework. In the reduced longitudinal network, the strongest evidence emerged in the contemporaneous and between-person networks. At the same assessment occasion, worry and tension were positively associated with depressed mood, trouble sleeping, irritability, difficulty concentrating, and financial difficulties. At between-person level, higher average worry was associated with higher average tension, depressed mood, and financial difficulties; while higher average tension was associated with higher average irritability, worry, and difficulty concentrating. In the temporal network, financial difficulties significantly predicted higher subsequent worry but lower subsequent tension. Anxiety-related distress was centrally embedded within the EORTC QLQ framework, with worry serving as a key connector linking emotional, cognitive, sleep-related, and financial concerns. Potential leverage points for supportive care during chemotherapy were identified. ClinicalTrials.gov ID NCT05838638; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05838638?term=NCT05838638&rank=1 .

papers.title: Mapping the global landscape of research on primary and secondary headaches from 2000 to 2025: a bibliometric analysis.
papers.abstract: To map research on primary and secondary headaches, including its interface with dentistry, in PubMed records entered in 2000-2025. PubMed records were retrieved with two strategies based on the International Classification of Headache Disorders and restricted to a validated thematic core; citations came from NIH iCite. Output, citation impact and flows, collaboration, co-citation and bursts of Medical Subject Headings were analyzed. Of 50,825 records, 40,441 formed the core (precision 92.0%; estimated sensitivity 99.2%). Annual output rose from 747 to 2,522 articles (modeled growth 4.0% annually), with a roughly stable MEDLINE share. The United States led production (29.8%) and China grew fastest. Migraine appeared in 68.7% of articles, secondary headaches in 12.2% and tension-type headache in 8.8%; the latter's share declined (odds ratio per decade 0.69; 95% confidence interval 0.65-0.72). Research shifted from triptans to calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) therapies, with bursts in CGRP antagonists, genetics and machine learning. The dental interface (temporomandibular disorders, bruxism, orofacial pain) appeared in 1.3% of articles; only 1.0% of all articles were in dental journals, which received one third of expected citations. Headache research grew with the biomedical literature and turned toward targeted therapies; tension-type headache is underrepresented given its prevalence, and the dental interface was small, with few articles in dental journals and limited uptake. Headache often coexists with temporomandibular disorders and sleep bruxism, yet few studies address dental aspects. The core journals and gaps identified can help dentists and researchers navigate the literature and identify research priorities.
